title: When an assumption becomes reality
dek: On the beliefs we stop noticing, and why it's worth asking where they came from.
body:
An assumption can become so deeply embedded in our understanding of reality that we no longer recognise it as an assumption.

I find this interesting when I think about how we come to understand the world. Few of our beliefs are formed independently. Much of what we consider normal, acceptable or simply true has been shaped by where we grew up, the people around us and the information we've taken in.

Consider how we define success. For many people, a successful life means financial security, career progression, home ownership and material possessions. These are reasonable things to value. But where did we get the idea that they're what a successful life is built on?

We rarely stop to examine these ideas. They're reinforced through education, advertising, popular culture, family expectations and the institutions we're part of. Eventually, what began as one set of cultural values starts to feel like an objective measure of how life should be lived.

This isn't limited to our personal ambitions. It shapes how we read other people, how we form political opinions and how we make sense of what's happening around us.

Our access to information has made this more complicated. We're exposed to endless opinions, commentary and competing explanations, yet much of it reaches us through systems built to predict what will hold our attention. We can spend hours consuming information and still have a narrow understanding of the subject.

> It's entirely possible to become more confident in an opinion without becoming any better informed about it.

I think that distinction is worth sitting with. We often associate confidence with knowledge, familiarity with understanding and consensus with truth. But none of these pairs are the same thing.

An idea doesn't become objectively true because we've heard it a thousand times. A belief doesn't become our own simply because we can articulate it. And the fact that something has always been done a particular way doesn't mean there was never another possibility.

I'm not suggesting we should question everything or abandon the assumptions that get us through everyday life. That isn't practical or useful. But I do think we should be more aware of what our understanding of the world is built on.

Sometimes the most valuable question isn't whether we agree or disagree with an idea. It's whether we've ever properly examined why we believe it in the first place.
